w: Behind this Mannerist screen on Piazza Maggiore once stood a jumble of houses and shops, where bankers set up their banchi - money-changing tables - under a portico added in 1412. By 1565 the commune hired the architect Vignola to unify it all behind fifteen asymmetric arches. Two still lead into the old alleys behind.
s: A facade built to dress up a money-changers' alley
_facts: Renaissance-style palace facade on the eastern flank of Piazza Maggiore
site previously a jumble of houses/shops; portico added 1412; alleys of banchi (money-changer) businesses
present facade designed by Vignola, commissioned 1565-1568
asymmetric facade with 15 rounded arches (two larger, leading to the old alleys) and Composite pilasters

w: Construction began in 1267 on this Augustinian basilica, home to a community of friars who still worship here. Its real draw is tucked inside: the Bentivoglio Chapel, built for Bologna's ruling family and packed with Renaissance artworks - a private dynasty's chapel hiding inside a public monastery church.
s: An Augustinian basilica hiding a Renaissance chapel
_facts: historic Roman Catholic basilica serving a monastery of Augustinian friars
construction began 1267
houses the Bentivoglio Chapel, featuring numerous Renaissance artworks

w: Locals call this triangular piazza the Seven Churches Square, after the Basilica di Santo Stefano anchoring one side. Porticos run the other two, fronted by a 15th-century merchant house and the Palazzo Bolognini Amorini Salina, its facade studded with terracotta heads. Flea markets and concerts still fill the square.
s: The 'Seven Churches Square', still doing business
_facts: also known as Piazza delle Sette Chiese (Seven Churches Square)
pedestrian triangular piazza, porticoed on two long sides, Basilica di Santo Stefano on the short side
used for cultural events, flea markets and concerts
Palazzo Bolognini Amorini Salina noted for terracotta-head frieze; 'Case Tacconi' a 15th-century Bolognese merchant house

w: The Palazzo Galvani that houses this collection was once grimly nicknamed the Hospital of Death. Founded in 1881 by merging the university's antiquities collection with the city's own finds, it grew into one of Italy's premier archaeological museums, with an Egyptian collection ranked among Europe's finest.
s: A museum of ancient bones in the old 'Hospital of Death'
_facts: housed in the 15th-century Palazzo Galvani, once known as the Hospital of Death
founded September 1881 merging the University of Bologna's antiquities room (est. 1714) with the city's collection
among the most important archaeological museums in Italy, prehistoric to Roman age
Egyptian collection among the most important in Europe

w: In 1381 Bologna's notaries - the guild keeping the city's contracts straight - built themselves a palace on Piazza Maggiore, crenellated brick beside the cathedral and city hall. Fioravanti remade one wing around 1437, Rubbiani restored the rest in 1908; 15th-century frescoes still line the inside.
s: Bologna's notaries built themselves a palace too
_facts: faces Piazza Maggiore, between the Basilica of San Petronio and Palazzo d'Accursio
built 1381 as the seat of the city's notaries guild, designed by Cavalletto and da Bagnomarino
section remade by Bartolomeo Fioravanti c.1437; restored 1908 by Alfonso Rubbiani
brick, crenellated top; interior has 15th-century frescoes

w: Carthusian monks founded this charterhouse in 1334; it was suppressed in 1797 and reborn in 1801 as Bologna's Monumental Cemetery, grand enough that Byron wrote admiringly of it. Then in 1869, workers hit something far older: an Etruscan necropolis in continuous use from the sixth to third centuries BC.
_facts: former Carthusian charterhouse, founded 1334, suppressed 1797
became Bologna's Monumental Cemetery in 1801, praised by Byron
Etruscan necropolis (6th-3rd century BC) discovered on site in 1869
located just outside the city walls, near Monte della Guardia and Stadio Renato Dall'Ara

w: Once the main seat of the University of Bologna, this palace now holds a municipal library and the Anatomical Theatre, where professors demonstrated dissections beneath carved wooden galleries to rows of students. At its heart survives a small university chapel, Santa Maria dei Bulgari, tucked between the stacks.
s: A dissection theatre and a chapel, tucked in a library
_facts: one of the most important buildings in Bologna, once the main University of Bologna building
now houses the Archiginnasio Municipal Library and the Anatomical Theatre
contains the university Chapel of Santa Maria dei Bulgari
